The applicant was born in 1964 and lives in Manisa, Turkey. He sat a competition for admission to the civil service in 1991. Following his success in the competition, the General Directorate of Higher Education Credit and Hostels Institution conducted a pre-employment background investigation. It found that the applicant had not mentioned his criminal record in his application form. In particular, in 1980 the applicant was convicted of issuing threats against one of his teachers and had been sentenced to four months and twenty days' imprisonment, which had then been converted into a fine. The applicant appealed the decision. On 28 December 1999 the Ankara Administrative Court awarded the applicant a certain amount of compensation for pecuniary damage.

The applicant, born in 1928, had a dispute with a ticket inspector, who accused her of having travelled without a valid ticket. When he was about to issue a penalty fare she refused to disclose her identity and the police were consequently called. They requested that the applicant give her name and address, and since she refused, she was arrested at 9.30 p.m. and brought to the police station. On 12 August 1995 at 10.45 a.m., the applicant revealed her identity. On 14 June 1996 the applicant claimed compensation for having been detained. The Chief Constable decided on the matter on 18 July 1996, and in so far as relevant his letter of the same day to the applicant reads as follows: “In connection with your previous complaint ... you received a ... letter of 14 September 1995 from Chief Superintendent HJH"

The applicant was arrested and held for 12 hours in a police station. The Chief Constable said that the length of her detention was due to her 'unwillingness to assist in replying to the question on which the police needed clarification' She complained against the decision to the Regional State Prosecutor in Viborg, who refused to grant her compensation. She appealed to the Prosecutor General, who upheld the decision on 25 November 1997. The applicant brought her claim for compensation before the City Court of Århus. A court session was held on 26 June 1998, in which she explained inter alia that she had refused to give her name to the ticket inspector partly because she was angry, partly because he already knew her.

The applicant did not appeal to the Ministry of Justice against the Chief Constable's decision, but on 31 July 1996 she complained against the decision to the Regional State Prosecutor in Viborg. The applicant appealed to the Prosecutor General, who upheld the decision on 25 November 1997. The prosecution maintained that the applicant's behaviour necessitated the arrest and the length of the detention. A court session was held on 26 June 1998, in which the applicant, represented by counsel, explained inter alia that she had refused to give her name to the ticket inspector partly because she was angry, partly because he already knew her. She alleged that the police did not question her or talk to her during the arrest, during the transportation to the police station, or after the arrival to the station.

The applicant was arrested after refusing to give her name and address to police officers. She was placed in a detention cell and denied medical treatment. The City Court decided that she had infringed section 750 of the Administration of Justice Act, which authorises the imposition of a fine. The officer who had been on duty on 12 August 1995 as from 6.30 a.m. stated inter alia that several times during the morning he send a colleague down to try to get the requested data from the applicant, but they only succeeded around 10.45 a. m., whereupon she was released. The duty officers were ordered, in the future, to appoint at the commencement of every duty period one among them to be responsible for the detainees.

The applicant, who screamed and appeared hysterical. at the police station she was brought before the officer on duty and again she refused to reveal her identity. She had not been in possession of any identification. The officer who had been on duty on 12 August 1995 as from 6.30 a.m. stated inter alia that several times during the morning he send a colleague down to try to get the requested data from the applicant. The City Court decided as follows: “As the [applicant] did not disclose her name and address to the two [named] police officers, she infringed section 750 of the Administration of Justice Act"

The applicant, who screamed and appeared hysterical, refused to reveal her identity. The officer who had been on duty on 11 August 1995 explained among other things that after repeated attempts to obtain the applicant's name and date of birth, he gave up and the applicant was thereafter placed in a waiting room. By judgment of 25 September 1998 the City Court decided as follows: “As the [applicant] did not disclose her name and address to the two [named] police officers, she infringed section 750 of the Administration of Justice Act, which authorises the imposition of a fine.” The duty officers were ordered, in the future, to appoint at the commencement of every duty period one among them to be responsible for the detainees.

The High Court of Western Denmark (Vestre Landsret) ruled that the applicant was entitled to compensation in the amount of DKK 2,200 pursuant to section 1018 a, subsection 1 of the Administration of Justice Act. The applicant's request of 24 February 1999 for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused by the Leave to Appeal Board (Procesbevillingsnævnet) on 25 May 1999. The prosecution appealed against the judgment to the High Court, before which the applicant admitted that the police had asked her before and after the arrest to provide them with her personal data, but she had refused because she had been angry.

The High Court of Western Denmark (Vestre Landsret) gave judgment against the applicant in 1999. The prosecution appealed against the judgment. The applicant's request of 24 February 1999 for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused by the Leave to Appeal Board (Procesbevillingsnævnet) on 25 May 1999. She is entitled to compensation in the amount of DKK 2,200 pursuant to section 1018 a, subsection 1 of the Administration of Justice Act. She was released as soon as she revealed her name and address. The court finds for the prosecution. No circumstances has been established, which could provide a basis for granting compensation.

The applicant was detained for breaching section 750 of the Administration of Justice Act. The High Court of Western Denmark ruled that she was entitled to compensation in the amount of DKK 2,200. The application for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused by the Leave to Appeal Board (Procesbevillingsnævnet) on 25 May 1999. The court found that there was no reason to extend the detention until the following day 11.00 a.m. The applicant admitted that police had asked her before and after the arrest to provide them with her personal data, but that she had refused because she had been angry.

The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court. By a decision of 30 April 2002 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The case was heard by the Court's First Section on 1 November 2001. The charge with the offence of refusing to reveal her identity was not followed up by an indictment. The outcome of the applicant's dispute with the bus company is unknown. The length of her stay in the detention cell from 11.00 p.m. until your release the following day, totalling 12 hours, can be ascribed substantially to your conduct and unwillingness to assist in replying to the question on which the police needed clarification. This decision can be appealed against to the Ministry of Justice... The claim for compensation made by you as regards the detention is yet to be heard. The Chief Constable decided on the matter on 18 July 1996, and in so far as relevant his letter of the same day to the applicant reads as follows: “In connection with your previous complaint ... you received a ... letter of 14 September 1995 from Chief Superintendent HJH [My] reply to your complaint... will not differ essentially from the content of [that letter].” The applicant did not appeal to the Ministry of Justice against the Chief Constable's decision, but on 31 July 1996 she complained against the decision to the Regional State Prosecutor in Viborg, who refused to grant her compensation. The applicant appealed to the Prosecutor General, who upheld the decision on 25 November 1997. A court session was held on 26 June 1998, in which the applicant, represented by counsel, explained inter alia that she had refused to give her name to the ticket inspector partly because she was angry, partly because he already knew her. She alleged that the police did not question her or talk to her during the arrest, during the transportation to the police station, or after the arrival to the station. The applicant had not been attended to by a doctor in connection with her placement in the detention cell. The City Court decided as follows: “As the [applicant] did not disclose her name and address to the two [named] police officers, she infringed section 750 of the Administration of Justice Act, which authorises the imposition of a fine.” The prosecution appealed against the judgment to the High Court of Justice in Copenhagen, which upheld the City Court's decision. The applicant is entitled to compensation in the amount of DKK 2,200 pursuant to section 1018 a, subsection 1 of theadministration of justice Act. The applicant admitted that the police had asked her before and after the arrest to provide them with her personal data, but that she had refused because she had been angry. Two of the police officers who were heard as witnesses before the City Court repeated their testimonies. The applicant's request of 24 February 1999 for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused by the Leave to Appeal Board (Procesbevillingsnævnet) on 25 May 1999. On 11 February 1999 the High Court gave judgment against the applicant stating as follows: “Having breached section 750 of the Administration of Justice Act [the applicant] could be arrested pursuant to section 755”

The case was brought by a resident of Tettnang in the Land of Baden-Württemberg. He was ordered to pay a levy of 75 German marks (DM) by the local authority. He argued that it was contrary to the principle of equality before the law. The Court of Appeal ruled that the law is consistent with the Constitution. The case was dismissed on 18 August 1983. The court said there had been no change in the law on the matter since then. The decision was upheld by the High Court of Justice on 20 August 1984. The appeal was dismissed again on 16 August 1986. The matter was then referred back to the Court of Appeals for reconsideration. The High Court again ruled in favour of the original decision.

The case was brought by a resident of Tettnang, in the German state of Baden-Württemberg. He was ordered to pay a levy of 75 German marks (DM) for his use of the fire service. He argued that this was contrary to the principle of equality before the law. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 16 August 1982. The case was appealed again on 18 August 1983. The Appeal Court again rejected the appeal, stating that there had been no change in the law since the original appeal was made. The appeal was rejected again on 20 July 2013. The matter has now been heard by the Court of Appeals of Germany.

The case involves an obligation to pay a levy to the German state of Baden-Wurttemberg. The court of appeal ruled that the obligation was compatible with the Constitution. The case was dismissed on appeal on 18 August 1983. The appeal was brought by a resident of the town of Tettnang who was forced to pay the levy because he was the only person in the town to do so. The decision of the Court of Appeal was that the requirement was consistent with the law and that there was no change in the law on the matter. The Supreme Court of Germany ruled in favour of the resident and the decision was overturned on appeal.

The applicant challenged this judgment, which had been delivered on 25 March 1986. The Federal Administrative Court dismissed his appeal on 6 October 1986. On 11 November 1986 Mr Schmidt applied finally to the Federal Constitutional Court, which on 31 January 1987, sitting as a panel of three members, declined to accept the appeal for adjudication. It noted that there had still been no general change in legal opinion. The fact that the obligation to serve in the fire brigade was limited to male residents of a municipality still continued to be objectively justified on account of the risks inherent in service in theFire Brigade. “The sole decisive factor is that there remain today objective reasons (Anknüpfungspunkte) on the basis of which the legislature is entitled to treat men and women differently in this regard. That does not mean that there is an obligation to enact regulations differentiating between the sexes. ...” says the court in Rhineland-Palatinate in a decision on the case of a fireman who was convicted of sexually assaulting a woman. The man was sentenced to two years in prison and a fine of up to $10,000; the sentence was suspended for two years and a $5,000 fine was suspended. The court also ruled that the woman could not be allowed to work as a firefighter.

Rhineland-Palatinate (section 10 para. 2 of the Rhineland- Palatinate Fire Protection Act) make provision for an obligation to serve in the fire brigades regardless of sex. The sole decisive factor is that there remain today objective reasons (Anknüpfungspunkte) on the basis of which the legislature is entitled to treat men and women differently in this regard. That does not mean that there is a obligation to enact regulations differentiating between the sexes. ...“That doesn't mean there is an obligation for the legislature to enact laws differentiating among the sexes,” the court said.

The decision was based on section 43 of the Land Fire Brigades Act, as amended on 27 November 1978 (Feuerwehrgesetz) and on the municipal decree (Satzung) of 5 December 1979. The decision of the Administrative Court to impose a fire service levy on men was overturned. The case was referred back to the Constitutional Court. The Constitutional Court ruled that the levy was not in breach of the Constitution. The Administrative Court was not able to overturn the decision. The decision to impose the fire service tax was upheld by the Court of Appeal on 6 October 1986. The matter was returned to the Federal Constitutional Court for reconsideration. The appeal was rejected again on 8 October 1986 and the decision was appealed again on 18 August 1987. The final decision was returned on 8 November 1987 and the case was dismissed on 9 November 1987. This is the last appeal against the decision to force men to pay fire tax. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept the appeal for adjudication, on the ground that it did not have sufficient prospects of success. Mr Schmidt applied to the court in 1986, but there was no evidence of new facts or a fundamental change in legal opinion. Some fire brigade duties were performed by women and recently fire brigades for female volunteers had even been set up. But this did not mean that there was an obligation to enact regulations differentiating between the sexes, the court said. The sole decisive factor is that there remain objective reasons (Anknüpfungspunkte) on the basis of which the legislature is entitled to treat men and women differently in this regard.

The applicant was born in 1952 and lives in Mardin. He was arrested and taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation on 22 December 1980. On 19 February 1985 the Diyarbakır Martial Law Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to twenty-four years' imprisonment. On 29 July 1990 the applicant was released from detention. On 10 September 1998 the judgment became final in respect of the applicant. The case was subsequently dismissed on the grounds that the time limit under Articles 102 and 104 of the Criminal Code had expired. The applicant's case was eventually dismissed on 13 July 1998 on the ground that the offence fell within the scope of Article 168 § 2.

He was also ordered to pay an additional fine of ATS 10,000 as he had already been order to pay ATS 25,000 in four other sets of disciplinary proceedings. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) about the length of the proceedings and claimed that the disciplinary authorities had failed to take the excessive length into account as a mitigating circumstance. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint on 29 February 2000. This decision was served on the applicant on 6 April 2000.

In 1982 the Supreme Court of Sweden ruled that a person cannot be taxed for more than two years without having to pay the full amount of the tax owed. The case was decided in favor of the person’s claim that he was not entitled to the full tax rate. The judge ruled that the person did not have to pay more than the amount owed under the law. The court made the decision in favour of the man's claim that the tax was too high. The Supreme Court ruled that he should pay less than the full rate due to lack of ability to pay for two years. The man was given a year to pay back the tax, which he did.

In 1982 the Supreme Court of Sweden ruled in favor of a tax break for people who live in the north of Sweden who work in the south of Sweden. In March 1983 the decision was overturned by the Court of Appeal of Sweden, which ruled the tax break did not apply to those who lived in the South of the Swedish mainland. In October 1984 the court again ruled in favour of tax break, this time only for those living in the North. The South of Sweden is the only part of the country not affected by the ruling. The rest of the nation is subject to the same rule, with the exception of a few states, such as Norway, Sweden, Norway and Finland.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 48983/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their plots of land were illegally seized by the administration for a dam construction without any payment, and requested compensation. The court ordered the administration to pay the applicants an amount of increased compensation, plus interest at the statutory rate, starting from 1986 when the land was submerged in the waters of the dam. On 6 October 1994 the Court of Cassation quashed these judgments, holding that the authorities had paid the resulting amounts to the owners registered in the local land registry. The Baskil Civil Court ordered the administration to pay the applicants a certain amount of compensation, plus interest running from 1986. The Court of Cassation reversed its decision and held, on 10 March 1995, that the cases could in fact be characterised as compensation claims arising from expropriation. On 9 December 1998 the administration paid TRL 934,027,000 to Ms Mürvet Fidan, 884,579,000 TRL to Mr Murat Fidan and 708,190,000 Turkish liras to Mr Hikmet Fidan. On 17 March 1998 the Court ofCassation upheld these judgments.

The applicant complained of the lack of legal recognition of her change of gender and the refusal of the Department of Social Security to pay her a retirement pension at the age of 60 as was the case for other women. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 19 May 2005, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required.

The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of the lack of legal recognition of her change of gender and the refusal of the Department of Social Security to pay her a retirement pension at the age of 60. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The case was settled by a decision of 19 May 2005, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The decision was made under the rules of Rule 52 of the Rules of Court.

Aged 24, she gave up attempting to live as a man, and had gender reassignment surgery two years later. She has presented as a woman since 1963. She paid contributions to the National Insurance scheme at the female rate (until 1975, when the difference in rates was abolished) In 1972 she became self-employed and started paying into a private pension fund. She applied to the local government benefits office for State pension payments. She wished these to commence on 22 December 1997, her 60th birthday. Her application was refused by a decision of the Adjudication Officer.

In the Court of Appeal, the applicant sought, inter alia, a declaration that she was entitled to her full retirement pension from her 60th birthday, and damages for breach of the Human Rights Act 1998, in force from 2 October 2000. Her case was adjourned to await the House of Lords judgment in Bellinger v. Bellinger. In that case the claimant, a transsexual, sought a declaration of validity in respect of a marriage contracted following gender reassignment surgery. On 26 April 2005 the applicant was issued with a Gender Recognition Certificate following her application under the Gender recognition Act 2004. The Government further refused to make any ex gratia payment of a sum representing her lost State pension.

At this time she claimed that she was no longer able to work due to a spinal collapse fracture of osteoporotic origin. Her case was adjourned to await the House of Lords judgment in Bellinger v Bellinger. The applicant was issued with a Gender Recognition Certificate on 26 April 2005. She had applied for recognition under the Genderrecognition Act 2004 which had come into force on 1 July 2004. train_texts: The case was brought to the Court of Appeal by the City of Berlin. The application was brought under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The court decided to rule on the merits of the application at the same time. The case was decided in favour of the city of Berlin, who won the case. The decision was published in the newspaper, Die Zeit, on 1 May 2005. The article was published under the heading ‘The Case for Human Rights’. The case was brought to the Court of Appeal under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the case at the same time. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Germany, which ruled in favor of the applicant. The decision was made by a majority of the court, which was the same as the decision made by the High Court of Justice. The court also ruled that the case was not in breach of the human rights of the citizens of Germany. The High Court ruled that there was no evidence of a breach of human rights. The judge ruled in favour of the application.

The case was brought under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The case was heard by the European Court of Human rights (ECHR) on 2 May 2005. The ECHR ruled that the case should be admitted into the European Convention on Human Rights. The ECHR ruled on the merits of the case on 3 May 2005, and the case was returned to the ECHR. The application was dismissed on 8 May 2005 by the ECHR, but the decision was appealed. The appeal was rejected on 10 May 2006. The case has been referred to by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) as a matter of ‘international concern’.

The applicant was born in 1944 and lives in Berlin. She worked as a ballet dancer for the Erich-Weinert-Ensemble (EWE) from 1960 to 1979. In 1979 she terminated her career on stage and worked for the company as a set and costume designer. The EWE paid the applicant her wages as a costume and set designer and, in addition, a monthly allowance in the amount of 588 GDR marks (hereafter ‘the allowance’) The allowance was paid by virtue of the regulation of the Minister of Culture of the German Democratic Republic (GDR) of 1 September 1976. On 1 January 1992 the Ministry discontinued all allowance payments to former ballet dancers. In December 1992 the applicant brought an action with the Berlin Social Court claiming the payment of the allowance.

The applicant subsequently lodged an appeal on points of law. In 2002, the Federal Constitutional Court delivered a leading decision. It ruled that the pension rights acquired in the GDR fell within the scope of Article 14 of the German Basic Law protecting the right to property provided that the right was transferred into the united German legal system. The case was settled at the Supreme Court of Germany.

The dancer's case was referred to the Frankfurt/Oder Labour Court. The wording of the pertinent provision of the German Unification Treaty was ambiguous. The provision could be interpreted as setting 31 December 1991 as the final date to qualify for the allowance or as terminating permanently the allowance payments from that date onwards. The allowance was paid out of public funds and was an atypical benefit granted by the GDR. Therefore it would have been necessary to rule explicitly that the allowance was to be transferred into the united German legal system. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint of approximately fifty pages with the Federal Constitutional Court. She complained that the length of the proceedings - which were still pending before the Federal Labour Court - violated Article 6 of the Convention.

The judge ruled that the former dancer should receive an old-age allowance. The decision was made under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, which applies to anyone who worked in the GDR from 1959 to 1971. The case was heard by the German High Court, which ruled in favour of the dancer's claim that she should be entitled to an old age pension. The court's decision was appealed to the High Court of Justice, who ruled against the dancer. The allowance was supposed to end on December 31, 1991. The court ruled that it was not the end of the allowance. It was only the cessation of the payment of the remainder of the annual allowance. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 24746/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his son Pearse Jordan had been unjustifiably shot and killed by a police officer. He invoked Articles 2, 6, 13 and 14 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. It was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building on 4 April 2000. The case was heard in tandem with three other cases brought by the Northern Ireland Human Rights Commission.

The applicant had climbed on the cupboard in her cell and passed the night thereon, failing to comply with the police’s order to descend. On 9 November 2008 the applicant was allowed to stay outside on those premises without being shackled. She was further allowed to receive three visits from a friend and two from her doctor C. The Lüneburg District Court dismissed the applicant's action of 8 November2008 under section 19 § 2 of the Lower Saxony Public Security and Order Act (see paragraph 43 below) The District Court confirmed that the detention had complied with section 18 § 1 no. 2 of the Lower Saxony Public Security and Order Act. The photographs of shackled persons exposed in the detention wing of the Braunschweig Police Station may have been tasteless, but did not render the applicant’s detention unlawful as a result of intimidation. The recommendations of the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CPT) were irrelevant here. The fact that the light had remained switched on all night in Braunshweig had been a consequence of the applicant's own behaviour. The light had therefore been necessary for her own protection. The Lüneburg Regional Court dismissed the applicant's appeal against the District Court’s decision of 15 July 2009. The Regional Court, endorsing the findings in its decision of 7 November 2008, confirmed that the applicant’'s detention as such had complied with section 18 § 1 no. 2 of the Lower Saxony Public Security and Order Act. The applicant had not substantiate that her state of health in detention had deteriorated in a manner so as to render her detention disproportionate. The doctor who had visited the applicant in detention and persuaded the then competent District Court judge to order her release had probably been a sympathiser. In that police station there were no detention cells suitable for a deprivation. The Regional Court noted that the applicant arrived at that station on 8 November 2008 at 2.10 a.m. after the crew of the ambulance called by the police and a police doctor had confirmed her fitness for detention. The court considered that it had been lawful for the police to leave the light switched on during the night. The applicant had climbed on a cupboard measuring 1.90 metres and had failed to descend on the police’s request. By choosing not to descend her by force and by leaving the light on instead the police had respected as much as possible the applicant's right to liberty. The Regional Court found that the right provided by no. 10 of the Police Custody Regulations to be allowed to stay outside for 45 minutes per day in so far as the staffing and infrastructural situation permitted had not been breached. The Regional Court observed that under no. 11 of the Police Custody Regulations such visits were permitted in so far as they did not endanger the purpose of the detention. The Regional Court noted that the Braunschweig Police had received some 200 telephone calls of sympathisers of the applicant, some of whom had insulted the police. It had not been unlawful in these circumstances for the police not to permit visits by persons who had presented themselves at the police station without having lodged a request for a visit. In any event, the applicant had been visited by three persons while in detention, in addition to the two visits by her doctor, C., who had prescribed her necessary medication and had brought a couple of magazines. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the complaint on 28 October 2009. On 18 June 2012 the court decided to take no further action. The case is still pending and is expected to be heard again on 23 August 2013. The complaint was brought by a group of lawyers and academics. The court’s decision was made on the basis of the evidence that was presented to the court. The decision was based on the fact that the case was brought on behalf of a class of people who had been denied the right to defend their right to sue the government. The claim was that they had been deprived of their constitutional right to challenge the law in court, and that they were not entitled to a response.

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 28 October 1996. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr J.M. Morenilla, the elected judge of Spanish nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 September 1997. Mr Thór Vilhjálmsson replaced, as President of the Chamber, Mr Ryssdal who was unable to take part in the further consideration of the case. The facts underlying the procedure in issue were described in the judgment of the Saragossa Audiencia Provincial of 6 November 1991. Mr Tejedor García, who was born in 1948, was an officer in the national police force and lived at Mataró (Barcelona) At the material time, he was in Gallur (Saragossa) where he joined members of his family and friends to celebrate his niece’s first communion. At about 8.30 p.m., after a banquet which followed the ceremony and at which he drank, in addition to the wine that accompanied the meal, three glasses of champagne, a cognac and two half-measures of the wine, he drank. Manuel Tejedor García shot a shot into the ceiling of a Gallur café. He kicked Mr Leonel Pajucides in the testicles after throwing the latter’s identity card to the floor saying that it was ‘shit’ Pointing his revolver at the two Africans, he forced them to leave the café with their hands above their heads and took them to the guardia civil barracks, where, finally, he handed them over to the officers on duty. These events provoked the indignation and disapproval of the people present who gathered round the police officer and his prisoners after following them from the café. A preliminary inquiry was opened in respect of the applicant for wrongful arrest, assault and disobeying orders. The ANPU (Asociación Nacional de la Policía Uniformada) brought a private prosecution against the guardia civil officers of Gallur. It requested the court to declare that the applicant was innocent, and to investigate the responsibility of the two officers who had arrested him. On 10 September 1990 the investigating judge, having regard to the contradictory evidence as to the assault and the offer of drugs to the applicant, considered that no offence had been made out and decided, in accordance with Article 789 of the CCP (see paragraph 16 below) In an annotation of 7 November 1990 the registrar attested that the public prosecutor had returned the case file and lodged an application for the decision to be set aside (recurso de reforma) or, in the alternative, an appeal (see paragraph 16 below), dated 13 September 1990. On the following day, the decision was served on Mr Gallego. However, no annotation appears on the file attesting service on the publicProsecutor. In a decision (auto) of 4 December 1990 the investigating judge rejected MrGallego’s observations and held that the application had been made in time. As to the merits he stated that it would be better to test the evidence at an adversarial. On 12 February 1991 the investigating judge made a final discontinuance order in respect of the two guardia civil officers accused by the ANPU. On 6 November 1991 the Audiencia Provincial dismissed the preliminary objection that the public prosecutor’s application had been made out of time and found the applicant guilty of the alleged offences. It sentenced him to six months and fifteen days’ imprisonment, and a fine of 200,000 pesetas, and ordered him to pay compensation to the victims. On 28 May 1993 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. It found that there was nothing in the case file to show when it had been sent to the publicProsecutor or when the public Prosecutor had been served with the decision. The Constitutional Court ruled that the application was not in breach of the law. The court said the application had been filed after the law had been changed. It said the new interpretation was consistent with the new law and would not have affected the original application. The decision was made on the basis that the law was clear and the application did not need to be re-applied. The case was dismissed and the appeal was rejected on the grounds that it did not meet the requirements for an appeal to be heard in court. The appeal was dismissed on the ground that it was an appeal against a decision that was already made by the court and was therefore not necessary.

Spaniards shall be equal before the law and may not be discriminated against in any way on account of birth, race, sex, religion, opinion or any other condition or personal or social circumstance. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 7 April 1993 and by the Government of the Austrian Republic (“the Government”) on 14 May 1993. It originated in an application (no. 13470/87) against Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 6 October 1987 by a private association with legal personality under Austrian law. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality. The applicant, Otto-Preminger-Institut für audiovisuelle Mediengestaltung (OPI), is a private association under Austrian law established in Innsbruck. It is a non-profit-making organisation, its general aim being to promote creativity, communication and entertainment. Its activities include operating a cinema called “Cinematograph’ in Innersbruck, Austria. The applicant association announced a series of showings, which would be accessible to the general public, of the film Das Liebeskonzil (“Council in Heaven’) The Court heard their addresses as well as replies to its questions. The first of these showings was scheduled for 13 May 1985. All were to take place at 10.00 p.m. except for one matinée performance on 19 May. The public prosecutor instituted criminal proceedings against OPI’s manager, Mr Dietmar Zingl. The charge was “disparaging religious doctrines’ (Herabwürdigung religiöser Lehren), an act prohibited by section 188 of the Penal Code (Strafgesetzbuch - see paragraph 25 below). The film had been shown at a private session in the presence of a duty judge (Journalrichter) before the public prosecutor made an application for its seizure. Public showings announced by OPI could not take place. Mr Zingl had returned the film to the distributor, the “Czerny’ company in Vienna. It was in fact seized at the latter’s premises on 11 June 1985. A trial took place before the Innsbruck Regional Court on 10 October 1986. The film was again shown in closed session; its contents were described in detail in the official record of the hearing. The wholesale derision of religious feeling outweighed any interest the general public might have in information or the financial interests of persons wishing to show the film. The Regional Court found it to be established that the distributor of the film had waived its right to be heard and had agreed to the destruction of its copy. The film Das Liebeskonzil, in which God the Father is presented both in image and in text as a senile, impotent idiot, Christ as a cretin and Mary Mother of God as a wanton lady, came within the definition of the criminal offence of disparaging religious precepts. The court’s reasoning included the following: “The conditions of section 188 of the Penal Code are objectively fulfilled by this portrayal of the divine persons ...” The limitations on artistic freedom are to be found, firstly, in other basic rights and freedoms guaranteed by the Constitution (such as the freedom of religion and conscience), secondly, in the need for an ordered form of human coexistence based on tolerance. Mr Zingl appealed against the judgment of the Regional Court, submitting a declaration signed by some 350 persons. The Innsbruck Court of Appeal declared the appeal inadmissible on 25 March 1987. The Attorney General decided on 26 July 1988 that there were no grounds for filing such a plea of nullity. The decision mentioned, inter alia, that the Attorney General’s Department (Generalprokuratur) had long held the view that artistic freedom was limited by other basic rights. There have been theatre performances of the original play in Austria since then: in Vienna in November 1991, and in Inns bruck in October 1992. He was sentenced to nine years and six months in prison and imposed an accumulated prison sentence (Gesamtfreiheitsstrafe) of 9 years and 6 months. O. and P. were friends of L., one of the victims of the crime committed in Kassel on 14 October 2006, and they had both worked for some time as prostitutes in the Kassel apartment rented by L. before moving to Göttingen. The two men reported to the residual members of the criminal gang that they had spotted a safe in the apartment’s kitchen. Fearing for her life O. opened the safe from which B. removed EUR 300 and also handed over the contents of her wallet in the amount of EUR 250. B. left the apartment at around 8.30 p.m. taking the money. The Regional Court based its finding of facts regarding the first crime committed in Kassel on the statements made by the victims L. and I. on the occasion of their police interrogations as well as in the course of the subsequent trial. Both witnesses had identified the applicant without any hesitation as the perpetrator who had carried the gun when presented with his photo. It was also noted that at the investigative stage there had been no indication that the witnesses would refuse to repeat their statements at a subsequent trial. The Regional Court said that O. and P. had given detailed and coherent descriptions of the circumstances of the crime. Minor contradictions in their statements could be explained by their concern not to disclose their illegal residence status and activities to the authorities. The court observed that the witnesses’ attention during the incident had been focussed on the further perpetrator carrying the knife and that the applicant himself had only stayed a short period of time in the apartment. Their inability to identify the applicant also showed that the Witnesses, as opposed to the defence’s allegations, had not testified with a view to incriminating him. The fact that the detailed description of the events in the pre-trial statements were consistent with the account they had given the morning after the crime to their neighbour E. was a further strong indication for their credibility and the veracity of their statements. The Regional Court noted that neither the defence nor the court itself had had an opportunity to observe the main witnesses’ demeanour at trial or by means of an audio-visual examination. The court further emphasised that when taking into account the testimonies given by the witnesses' neighbour E. and their friend L. it had paid special attention to the fact that their statements constituted hearsay evidence and had to be assessed particularly carefully. The link between the evidence obtained in the course of such separate investigations and the crime at issue could only be made after O. and P. had reported the incident of 3 February 2007 to the police. A Swedish national, X, was a celebrity and a well-known television personality in Sweden. In October 2006 the applicant brought a private prosecution against X for gross defamation, claiming damages in the amount of 250,000 Swedish kronor (SEK; approximately 27,000 euros) X disputed the claim on the grounds, inter alia, that he was not the responsible editor of the show. In a preliminary ruling on 20 May 2008 the Stockholm District Court (Stockholms tingsrätt) dismissed the claim in so far as it was based on the Constitutional Law. It referred to the Supreme Court judgment in an almost identical case, NJA 2002 p. 314. The programme had first been sent by satellite link to Viasat Broadcasting UK Ltd, the British company responsible for the programme content, and thereafter uplinked to a satellite, which had in turn transmitted the programme to viewers in Sweden. As Chapters 1-9 of the Constitutional Law were not applicable, X could not be held responsible under Chapter 6. The applicant appealed and referred to his earlier submissions. The Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt) upheld the District Court’s decision. It held that the issue for it to determine was whether or not the broadcasting of the programme could be considered to have originated from Sweden within the meaning of Chapter 1, section 6(2) of that law. The applicant was convicted of aggravated fraud as well as tax and bookkeeping offences and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment. The criminal proceedings were finalised by a Supreme Court decision to refuse leave to appeal on 4 October 2010. These proceedings, in particular their compliance with Articles 6 and 7 of the Convention, are the subject of an application lodged with the Court on 4 April 2011 (no. 32814/11) The applicant subsequently withdrew his remaining claims before the District Court since there was no practical prospect of success in a continued procedure. The functions of District Attorneys carry out three different functions. The investigation (instruction) of criminal cases comes within the competence of the prosecuting authorities. eval_texts: The case was brought by a group of former employees of the company that owns the land where the site is located. They claim that they were denied the right to work because they were not paid in full. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), which ruled in favour of the workers. The ECHR ruled that the workers had not been treated fairly, and that they should not have been paid in the first place. The ECHR issued a ruling in favor of the employees, which the ECHR interpreted to mean that they had been denied their right to receive pay for their time worked on the site. The decision was made to dismiss the case, and the case was returned to the ECHR. Workers at the company in question worked overtime of 139.5 hours in months which had thirty-one calendar days and 135 hours in the remaining months. Work schedule did not take account of weekends or public holidays as duty‑free shops remained open twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week. The hours worked in excess of the regular forty-five-hour working week were paid at one and a half times the regular hourly rate. The court decided to join each applicant’s proceedings and to seek an expert report concerning the calculation of their claims for overtime, weekend and public holiday pay and remuneration for unused annual leave. Employer had previously been cautioned, on 25 November 1996, by the Ministry of Labour concerning its practices on working hours. On the basis of his examination of the company’s timekeeping records, the expert calculated the number of hours worked as overtime in respect of each applicant, deducting three hours of rest per each day worked. Expert determined that the employer did not owe anything to the applicants for weekend and public holiday work as the remuneration for those days had been in accordance with the applicable regulations. Expert also noted that the applicants could not claim any compensation for unused annual leave as they were still working at the company and such leave was only payable at the end of a contract. Both parties appealed to the Court of Cassation. In September 2005 the İzmir Labour Court found in favour of the applicants in part and awarded them the amounts given in the expert’s report in respect of the unpaid overtime. On 17 April 2006 the Court Of Cassation quashed the decision and remitted the case. It found that the Labour Court had not taken into account any time that could have been used for rest periods and that therefore the calculation of overtime could not be deemed accurate. It also stated that the overtime calculation should be based on weekly working hours rather than the monthly working time used in the Expert report. The applicants' daily working time was calculated as 14 hours. The Court of Cassation had ruled that working for more than 14 hours a day was physically impossible. The applicants appealed against the decision and maintained that the fact that they had worked continuously for twenty-four hours had already been confirmed by the legal records of the Ministry of Labour. On 18 March 2010 the Court ofCassation upheld the İzmir Labour Court’s decision without responding to the applicants’ objections. Some of the applicants' claims were dismissed entirely, while the others were awarded almost ninety percent less than the previous expert report had calculated. In the end, the applicants were not awarded any overtime.

U.S. Department of State repeatedly requested information as to which steps had been taken to locate the second applicant and to enforce the return order of 20 December 1995. Article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention made clear that the child's well-being took priority over the Convention's general aim of preventing child abduction. Reasons of general deterrence or, in other words, the aim of showing that child abduction was not worthwhile could not justify exposing a child to a grave risk of physical or psychological harm, the court said. In the main proceedings, the courts had denied that there was any risk of psychological harm (as a result of the alleged sexual behaviour of the first applicant) exclusively on account of the child's tender age. In these circumstances, it could not be excluded that the child, who was now more than two years old and had been living solely with her mother for more than a year, would suffer grave psychological harm in the event of a return to her father. The Regional Court had rightly found that the question whether the return order could be enforced by coercive measures needed further examination, including an opinion by an expert in child psychology. It might also prove necessary to assess whether or not the mother's allegations were at all true. The court ruled that the situation had changed fundamentally since the return order was issued on 20 December 1995. The second applicant had lost all contact with the first applicant and her ties with her mother and her maternal grandparents had become ever closer. The mother faced criminal prosecution in the United States and the child would, accordingly, be taken away from her. Article 16 of the Hague Convention, which prohibited the State to which the child has been abducted from taking a decision on custody while proceedings for the child's return were pending, no longer applied, as the decision not to enforce the returns order had become final. Following appeal proceedings the judgment became final on 31 March 1998.

Lord Steyn stated, inter alia, concerning the general principles: “Certain general propositions about the powers of constables under a section such as section 12(1) can now be summarised. (1) In order to have a reasonable suspicion the constable need not have evidence amounting to a prima facie case. (2) Hearsay information may therefore afford a constable reasonable grounds to arrested. Such information may come from other officers ... (3) The information which causes the constability to be suspicious of the individual must be in existence to the knowledge of the police officer at the time he makes the arrest. (4) The executive ‘discretion’ to arrest or not ... vests in the constables, who is engaged on the decision, and not in his superior officers. ‘A mere request to arrest without any further information by an equal ranking officer, or a junior officer, is incapable of amounting to reasonable grounds for the necessary suspicion’ ‘How can the badge of superior officers and the fact that he gave an order make a difference? ... In practice it follows that a constable must be given some basis for a request to arrested someone under a provision such as section 12(1), e.g. a report from an informer.’  ‘It is accepted, and rightly accepted, that a mere. request to Arrest without any Further Information by anequal ranking officer or a. junior officer is incapable. of amountING toreasonable grounds for a necessary suspicion.”

One of the police officers grabbed her, twisted her left arm behind her back and her head knocked against the corner of the window- ledge. She lost consciousness for a short while. When she came round, she found herself by the police car and noticed severe pain in her left shoulder, which was being pressed towards her back by one of the officers. The applicant had been very aggressive. She had suddenly calmed down and declared that she would come along when she had taken her daughter, whom he had assumed to be about twelve years old, to a neighbour. The police officers had agreed in order to avoid a further escalation of the events. They had followed the applicants to the back door of the house. The first applicant tried to close the door behind her but Police Constable Wildschut blocked the door open and pulled her outside. The child went upstairs. According to the report, Mrs KLAas struggled, struck out and tried to free herself from the police officer’s grip. The first applicant laid an information against the police officers concerned. She alleged that they had assaulted her contrary to Articles 223 and 230 of the Criminal Code. On 18 September 1986, the Head of the Detmold District Administration, acting as the Police Department authority (Kreispolizeibehörde), dismissed her complaint. The first applicant’s subsequent appeal to the Hamm Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) and to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht), were dismissed. Police Constable Wildschut was the next to give evidence. He confirmed the general circumstances of the first applicant’s arrest as described by Police Constable Bolte, although he was not prepared to say that she had run away. He could not remember who had kept hold of Mrs Klaas until they had put her into the police car, or whether she had bent forward suddenly owing, for instance, to a jerking on her handcuffs and the resulting pain. She had resisted arrest and had been lashing out when he had twisted her arm behind her back. She continued, without success, to resist accompanying them, but he could not be sure who had been holding on to her while they waited for the second police car. She said that she had managed to see through the plain glass door panel that one of the police officers had pushed her mother’s head against the wall. The officer concerned had blond hair. The plaintiff ended up with a graze on her temple, contusion of the left shoulder and probably also concussion, as was also confirmed in part by witnesses Bolte and Wildschut. These injuries were probably sustained by the plaintiff in the context of her arrest. It does not follow, however, that the defendant Land is liable in damages. Police officers found that the plaintiff’s breath smelt of alcohol. Even if the plaintiff had no intention whatsoever to abscond, the situation nevertheless appeared otherwise to the police officers. The arrest does not appear to be disproportionate either, but a perfectly reasonable means of ensuring that the further investigations could be carried out. It is for the plaintiff to prove that in this initially lawful exercise of their duty the police Officers went further than was necessary, by handling the plaintiff too roughly and in so doing injuring her or even by deliberately inflicting the injuries on her. The plaintiff, however, has not succeeded in providing such proof. With respect to the origin of the graze, the evidence of witness Monika Klaas, the plaintiff's daughter, conflicts. Mrs Klaas' claim that she was subjected in the course of her arrest to inhuman and degrading treatment by the police was dismissed by a court in 1989. A panel of three judges of the Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept for adjudication the first applicant’s constitutional complaint on the ground that it did not offer sufficient prospects of success. ‘The Chamber considers it by no means improbable that the plaintiff sustained all her injuries when she resisted being handcuffed. In the process her head could easily have knocked against the wall. The shoulder contusion could also have occurred when she struggled while being restrained by the. police and when the handcuffs were being put on her’ The Commission declared the applicants’ complaints admissible. The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the various separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. The Government in their memorial of 12 November 1992 invited the Court to find “that the applicants did not suffer violations of their rights under Article 3 or Article 8 (art. 8) of the Convention’”. The Court has ruled that the first applicant was entitled to the protection of her right to a fair trial. The second applicant was not entitled to that protection. The Commission found that no separate issue had arisen under Article 8. in respect of the first applicants.

The applicant fled Iraq and arrived at London Heathrow Airport on 30 December 2000. On arrival at the immigration desk he spoke to an immigration officer and claimed asylum. James Boyle was sentenced in Scotland to life imprisonment for murder in 1967. In March 1973, Mr. Boyle was removed from Peterhead Prison to a Special Unit in Barlinnie Prison. This Unit had been set up on an experimental basis to treat selected long-term prisoners and prisoners with violent propensities. The Unit had a maximum of eight prisoners and was characterised by a more liberal regime. In particular, he discovered that he had special abilities in working with people and in sculpture, writing and other areas of artistic activity. He was thereby able to meet his wife, talk to her on the telephone and correspond with her without being subject to the normal restrictions. The applicants’ complaints to the Commission in so far as relevant to the present proceedings all related to the period between September 1980 and November 1981 when Mr. Boyle was subject to the ordinary prison regime at Saughton Prison. The factors governing the choice included the desirability of his occupying a single cell rather than being in a dormitory; the availability of suitable day-time work for him and of facilities for continuing his studies and his artistic work; and access to suitable educational and vocational opportunities for his pre-release training. The applicants also asserted before the Commission that on occasions the prison censorship officer read out aloud in front of other inmates letters from Mrs Boyle. It originated in an application (no. 16817/90) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under Article 25 on 7 August 1989. The object of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 of the Convention. On 21 February 1997 the Court’s Screening Panel decided not to decline consideration. The applicants designated the lawyers who would represent them (Rule 31).

The first applicant is the mother of two children, P. and J.; the second applicant is J.’s father. The first applicant came into contact with the social authorities in 1984 while expecting her first child P. Following the birth of her second son J. in 1986 the first applicant and her sons returned to her parents. In the summer of 1986 she moved to Högsbohöjd. Since 1989 she has been living at Västra Frölunda in order to be closer to herParents. The children were placed at the Bö Children's Home in Gothenburg. In March 1989 the County Administrative Court ordered that the children be taken into care pursuant to section 1 of the Act containing Special Provisions on the Care of Young Persons 1980.

The first applicant is the mother of two children, P. and J.; the second applicant is J.’s father. The children were placed at the Bö Children's Home in Gothenburg. The first applicant appealed against the decision to take the children provisionally into care. However, the County Administrative Court and the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) upheld the decision and the Supreme Administrative Court (regeringsrätt) refused the applicant leave to appeal. The case was appealed to the Supreme Court of Sweden, which heard the case on May 23, 2008. The judge ruled in favour of the first applicant and ordered that the children be returned to her.

The first applicant’s access to her sons J. and P. was restricted after they were placed with foster parents on 7 March and 18 April 1989 in separate homes. From March 1989 until March 1990 she was in fact able to visit her children in the foster homes once every second week for 2½ hours. On 20 March 1990 the Chairperson of the Social Council (stadsdelsnämnden) of Högsbo decided, pursuant to section 16 of the 1980 Act (see paragraph 29 below), to restrict the first applicant's access. The first applicant appealed against the above decision to the County Administrative Court. She maintained primarily that the decision had been unlawful in that the social council had not been empowered to restrict access.

name: Wacław Płoski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26761/95) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the refusal to allow him to attend the funerals of his parents was in breach of Article 8 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 4 December 2001 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. It was decided that the application was not admissible and that the case was dismissed.

The applicant was born in 1949 and lives in Wrocław, Poland. He was arrested by the police on 22 February 1994 and charged with larceny. On 2 July 1994 the applicant’s mother died. The applicant made an application for leave to attend the funeral of his mother. The judge rejected the application on 5 July 1994. On 3 August 1994 his father died. On 6 August 1994 he applied for compassionate leave. The application was rejected on 9 August 1994. It was decided that “there are no compassionate circumstances as referred to in Art. 59 § 1 of the Code of the Enforcement of Sentences”

The applicant made an application for leave to attend the funeral of his mother on 3 July 1994. The judge rejected the application on 5 July 1994 because he was a habitual offender and a return to prison could not be guaranteed. The application was accompanied by a statement of a prison officer who supported the applicant's request. On 3 August 1994 the applicants father died. On 6 August 1994 he applied for leave for his mother's funeral.

Mr Wacław Płoski alleged, in particular, that the refusal to allow him to attend the funerals of his parents was in breach of Article 8. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section on 1 November 2001. By a decision of 4 December 2001 the Court declared the application partly admissible. In July 1994 the applicant made an application for leave to attend the funeral of his father. The judge rejected the application on the grounds that there were no compassionate circumstances. In August 1994, the applicant’s father died. The applicant then applied for compassionate leave to pay last respects to his father, who had also died in July 1994. The application was rejected on the basis that the applicant was a habitual offender whose return to the prison could not be guaranteed. He was sentenced to five years in prison for a drug-related offence. He served three and a half years of a five-and-a-half year sentence for a drugs-related offense. The application was accompanied by the statement of a prison officer who confirmed that the applicant’s “behaviour was beyond reproach” and that he “stayed in touch with his wife and children” The court gave the following reasons for its decision: “The charges against the accused involve a significant danger to society. The accused Wacław Płoski is a habitual offender within the meaning of Article 60 § 2 of the Criminal Code” On 26 May 1995 the applicant was convicted of larceny and received a prison term. The applicant was released from prison on 27 February 1996.

name: Edward Skałka
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that the proceedings were conducted by courts which lacked impartiality and alleged that his criminal conviction was in breach of Article 10. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 12 June 2001 the Court declared the complaint under Article 6 § 1 inadmissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section on 1 November 2001. The Court declared that the remainder of the application admissible on 3 October 2002.

The applicant was convicted of aggravated theft and sentenced to imprisonment. While in prison he wrote a letter to the Penitentiary Division of the Katowice Regional Court and he received a reply. Dissatisfied with that reply, on 15 November 1994 the applicant complained about the judge who had replied to his letter. The relevant passages of the applicant's letter read: “Not only does [the judge] write rubbish about my alleged request for a pardon, which my request was absolutely not, but he also intimidates me (...)” The prosecuting authorities lodged a case against the applicant on 31 January 1994. The applicant is currently serving a prison sentence.

The Sosnowiec District Court convicted the applicant of insulting a State authority and sentenced him to eight months' imprisonment. The court found that on 15 November 1994 the applicant had sent a letter to the President of the Katowice Regional Court in which he referred to all judges of the Regional Court's Penitentiary Division in an insulting and abusive manner as “irresponsible clowns”. The applicant had stated that he had not meant the court as a whole, but only one judge, and this in his personal, not professional, capacity. He maintained that the letter could only be regarded as an insult against a private person, but not a State institution.

The applicant was charged with proffering insults against a State authority at its headquarters or in public. He sent a letter to the President of the Katowice Regional Court. In this letter the applicant had insulted an unidentified judge and all judges of that court. The Sosnowiec District Court convicted the applicant of insulting a state authority and sentenced him to eight months' imprisonment. The court had regard to the results of the applicant's examination by psychiatrists who found that he could be held criminally responsible. The applicant had also stated that he was of the view that the opinions formulated in his letter were, in the circumstances of the case, correct.

Bielsko-Biała Regional Court upheld the first-instance court's decision. The court observed that the sentence was commensurate with the applicant's degree of guilt and with the seriousness of the offence. The applicant's lawyer had argued that the applicant had intended to insult a specific person. However, the impugned letter had largely exceeded the limits of acceptable criticism and was directly aimed at lowering the court in the public esteem. The legal assessment of the facts of the case was correct, and the sentence imposed corresponded to the degree of theApplicant's guilt. The Court also noted that he had a long criminal record, even though he had been assessed positively by the penitentiary services and could be held criminally responsible.

The sentence was commensurate with the applicant's degree of guilt and with the seriousness of the offence. The appeal was transferred to the Bielsko-Biała Regional Court. The court upheld the contested judgment, having examined both the appeal lodged by the applicant himself and that of his lawyer. The judge said that it was beyond any doubt that the applicant was the author of the letter.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13258/09) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Two Norwegian nationals, Mr Lars Lillo-Stenberg and Mrs Andrine Sæther (“the applicants”), alleged that their right to respect for private life had been breached by a Supreme Court judgment of 2 September 2008. The application was communicated to the Government, but it was decided to await the outcome of Von Hannover v. Germany ( no. 2) [GC], nos. 40660/08 and 60641/08, ECHR 2012. The applicants brought compensation proceedings against the magazine before Oslo District Court (Oslo tingrett) The magazine appealed to the Borgarting High Court (lagmannsrett), which by judgment of 13 February 2008 upheld the judgment. (34) In recent years the Supreme Court has considered legal questions relating to violation of privacy in the judgments Rt-2007-687 (Big Brother) and Rt -2008-489 (Plata). My argument is based mainly on these judgments. In my view, there is no need to consider whether, as contended by [Mr Justice U.S.], there is a need for an appeal. There is no reason for me to evaluate individual elements on the basis of whether or not they impinge on the concept of privacy. In this case it has been clearly established that the couple had not been informed beforehand that there were plans to publicise the wedding, nor were they asked for their consent. There would have been no question of violation of privacy if consent to publication had been obtained, cf. paragraph 62 of the judgment in the Big Brother case. The relationships within the family and between the family. and their friends are clearly of a personal nature. The article as a whole contains information about the couple and their child in addition to information about. the wedding. The next question is whether the article was unlawful. This question must be decided on the based of an overall evaluation of the article. The European Convention on Human Rights is incorporated into internal Norwegian law in the Human Rights Act. Both Article 8 relating to respect for private and family life and Article 10 relating to the right to freedom of expression are central to the present case. The central issue with respect to protection of privacy is therefore whether the published article contributes to a debate of public interest. In the assessment of legality, protection under Article 8 is the most relevant principle to be weighed. The article in question clearly has a purely entertainment value. Both [applicants] are well-known figures, but neither of them has had a prominent role either in the public administration or in any other public body. The Court of Human Rights in the case of von Hannover and the subsequent judgment of the Supreme Court in the Big Brother case have premises that seem to go far in support of protection against the use of pictures and texts concerning an individual’s private life. A wedding is a public affirmation that two persons intend to live together, and has legal consequences in many different sectors of society. Information about a wedding does not in itself involve a violation of privacy if it is given in a neutral form and based on a reliable source. That protection extends beyond the private family circle and also includes a social dimension. The Court considers that anyone, even if they are known to the general public, must be able to enjoy a ‘legitimate expectation’ of protection of and respect for their private life .... Se og Hør ran several articles featuring photos taken from different sources together with speculation and gossip. The magazine also described the relationship between the parties during their life together, which was an invasion of their private life as a couple. The right to protection of privacy is no weaker for well-known cultural personalities than it is for others, despite the fact that their photos are published in magazines and newspapers and on the internet. It could be said that in the case of such individuals it is even more important to ensure that their private lives and personal relationships are protected. (45) A wedding is a very significant personal experience for the bridal couple. The photos were taken from a headland about 200-250 metres from the islet where the ceremony was being held. A 300- to 400-millimetre zoom lens was used. The situation would not have been any better if the photography had taken place somewhere closer, or from a place where the photographer and journalist could have been seen by the wedding party. This could have disturbed the whole wedding. Many of the arrangements were such as to attract attention from third parties, for example the arrival of the bride in an open boat and the presence of a men’s choir singing a hymn. The photographs were taken of a wedding in a place accessible to the public. The article in Se og Hør also describes in words and pictures details of the wedding. together with the couple’s under-age child. The photo had previously been published in Aftenposten, and it has not been contended that consent was lacking on that occasion. The Court therefore allows the appeal. However, the case raises difficult and uncertain legal questions, clarification of which is in the public interest, cf. section 20-2, third paragraph, a, of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr Justice T. gave the following reasons which in the main were endorsed by the other member of the minority: “(58) I am substantially in agreement with the first-voting judge's general interpretation of section 3-6 of the Damages Act and section 390 of the Penal Code. (59) I will first examine whether the subject of the article can be considered to be ‘a personal matter’ in the meaning of section 390. Weddings have always been a subject of general interest in the sense that those close to the bridal couple consider them important and wish to participate. It is not unusual for the couple to wish to share their wedding and its arrangements only with those closest to them, and often to give the event a personal touch. In my view all the relevant circumstances indicate that in the present case the wedding was a private event. The wedding party was held at a hotel on Tjøme, which in this context is clearly a private area. The fact that there is a general right of public access to the islet does not prevent this part of the wedding from also being of a clearly private nature. The article included a description of the guests and the couple’s families, together with the names of well-known figures. I regard these as the personal touch that the bridal couple had wished to give their wedding and that in my view underlines the private nature of the wedding. In the present case the publication was a celebrity article written for the sole purpose of entertainment. Although the desire to entertain is in itself legitimate, its nature does not justify overriding the affected parties’ desire to protect their privacy. Well-known persons also have the right to respect for personal matters of the kind we are dealing with here. However, when matters of a personal nature such as those in question here are published, they must have at least a minimum of public interest if they are to be considered legitimate. Se og Hør’s use of a zoom lens enabled the journalist and the photographer to take close-up pictures of the bridal couple and their guests that make it look as if they were actually at the event themselves. The opposite parties have demanded that the amount decided by the Court of Appeal should be maintained. I have no objections to the amounts decided on. Since I know that I am in the minority, I will not formulate a final conclusion.” (70) For these reasons I am of the opinion that the article cannot be justified on the basis of an assessment of legality, and that the opposite parties are entitled to redress.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case was referred to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. On 12 January 1999 the Chamber decided to adjourn the examination of the applicant’s complaint concerning the length of the proceedings for rescission of the exclusion order. In a decision of 22 March 2000, the Grand Chamber declared the remainder of the application admissible, while reserving the issue of the applicability of Article 6 § 1 of the conventions. The applicant, who was born in 1958 in Tunisia, entered France in 1980 at the age of 22. On 14 September 1992 he married a French national, an invalid whose disability had been assessed at 80%. On 1 December 1988 the Alpes-Maritimes Assize Court sentenced the applicant to six years’ imprisonment for armed robbery and armed assault with intent for offences committed in 1985. On 8 August 1991 the Minister of the Interior made a deportation order against him. An appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 1 June 1994 on the ground that the applicant had failed to challenge the legality of the deportation order in the courts below. In December 1992 the applicant sought judicial review of the deportation order. In a judgment of 14 February 1994 the Nice Administrative Court quashed the order of 8 August 1991. The applicant applied to the Principal Public Prosecutor’s Office at the Aix-en-Provence Court of Appeal on 12 August 1994 for rescission of the ten-year exclusion order made by the Nice Criminal Court on 19 November 1992. He contended that he was married to a French national and held a provisional residence permit. On 4 September 1995 he was given a new three-month residence permit incorporating the right to seek employment. On 3 November 1997 the applicant was informed the case would be heard on 26 January 1998. The applicant received notice of a decision dated 2 April 1996 refusing him a residence permit. to live and work in France for a prolonged period, as he was married to a French citizen. He appealed to the Nice Administrative Court, but his appeal was dismissed on 27 September 1996. The applicant appealed on 24 December 1996 to the Lyons Administrative Court of Appeal. On 21 July 1998 the applicant obtained a temporary residence permit valid for one year. Recently he obtained a ten-year residence permit with the right to seek employment. The case is currently pending in the Marseilles Administrative Court Of Appeal – the court with jurisdiction – where the case is still pending.
