Three applicants were charged before the German courts with the commission of various criminal offences. Since they were not sufficiently familiar with the language of the country, they were assisted by an interpreter in accordance with German law. They consider that the inclusion of this latter item is contrary to, inter alia, Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention. The courts must use the services of an interpreter whenever the accused is not conversant with German. The same rule is applicable to the examination of witnesses who do not have command of the German language. The obligation to employ an interpreter is, however, subject to one exception.

Three applicants were charged before the German courts with the commission of various criminal offences. Since they were not sufficiently familiar with the language of the country, they were assisted by an interpreter in accordance with German law. They consider that the inclusion of this latter item is contrary to, inter alia, Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention. After conviction, the applicants were ordered, amongst other things, to pay the costs of the proceedings, including the interpretation costs. They say that this was contrary to the rules of German law and European Convention on Human Rights. They argue that the use of an interpreter by the courts in criminal proceedings is a violation of the convention. They claim that the courts must use an interpreter whenever the accused is not conversant with German.

The question of payment of the costs of the proceedings arises only after there has been a final ruling on the guilt of the accused. Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention, which forms an integral part of the domestic law, specifies that “everyone charged with a criminal offence has the (right) ... to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in court“ This text has not been interpreted and applied by the German courts in a uniform way. Certain courts read it as embodying an obligation for the Treasury to bear the costs in question for all time and in all cases.

Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, an accused person may never be required to make any advance payment on these costs. In the event of acquittal or of proceedings being discontinued, the Treasury in principle bears the costs. If the individual concerned is convicted, he has to pay the costs, but only such proportion thereof as relates to the criminal charges upheld by the court. Some courts read it as embodying an obligation for the Treasury to bear the costs in question for all time and in all cases. Other courts, including some higher courts, consider on the contrary that while Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) exempts an accused from paying in advance for the expenses incurred by the use of an interpreter, it does not prohibit such expenses being awarded against a convicted person.

Mohammed Belkacem is an Algerian citizen, born in 1954. He was involved in a dispute in a Berlin night-club during which another client lost his coat. His case was tried by the Berlin-Tiergarten Juvenile Court (Jugendschöffengericht) He was convicted of assault occasioning bodily harm and was ordered to pay the costs of the proceedings. On 10 April 1974, he filed an appeal against the order as to costs insofar as the interpretation costs had been included in the award. He submitted that Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention granted him exemption from payment of the costs in question. The Berlin Regional Court dismissed the appeal.

After completing his apprenticeship as a locksmith in Algeria, he rejoined his father in the Federal Republic of Germany where he followed various occupations. Berlin-Tiergarten Juvenile Court convicted Belkacem of assault occasioning bodily harm. He was sentenced to four weeks' imprisonment (Dauerarrest) and a fine of DM 500. The Berlin Regional Court dismissed the appeal. On 29 May 1975, his appeal was dismissed by the District Court which held that Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention granted him exemption from payment of the costs in question. The applicant unsuccessfully challenged the inclusion of interpretation costs in this assessment of the cost of the proceedings. The costs amount to DM 665.63, including DM 321.95 for interpretation costs. Arif Koç, a Turkish citizen born in 1940, has been employed in the Federal Republic of Germany in various trades, including mining and the construction industry. On 6 December 1973, the Assize Court attached to the Regional Court (Schwurgericht beim Landgericht) at Aachen convicted Mr. Koç of causing grievous bodily harm. He was sentenced to a year’s imprisonment, but the balance of his sentence remaining after allowance had been made for his detention on remand was commuted. On 5 May 1977, following a request by Mr. Belkacem, the Berlin Justizkasse allowed him to defer payment “until the decision of the Commission of Human Rights be known’ Cologne Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) set aside the Assize Court’s judgment insofar as it related to the interpretation costs. The object of the Convention is to secure human rights and fundamental freedoms against arbitrary State action and to place them under the protection of supranational law. The intention was to enshrine rights of the citizen and duties of the State which ensure a fair trial. A fair trial is guaranteed in this respect insofar as the accused must be assisted by the interpreter he needs. But it certainly does not mean that even a convicted person may not have the costs of interpretation awarded against him. According to the payment vouchers (Kassenanweisungen), the fees paid to the interpreter amounted to DM 311.50 for the hearing on 4 December 1973, DM 510.50 at 5 December and DM 112.50 on 6 December - making a total of DM 934.50. It cannot be assumed that the Convention is intended to provide a piecemeal solution of the question of costs in criminal proceedings. The Convention would not come appreciably nearer to achieving its aim by prohibiting a financial disadvantage of such a kind. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 23279/14) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the retrospective prolongation of his preventive detention breached his right to liberty under the Convention. The application was communicated to the Government on 17 June 2014. The Government were represented by two of their Agents, Mr H.-J. Behrens and Mrs K. Behr, of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection. The Court finds in favour of the applicant and orders the case to be dismissed. The German Government is entitled to appeal the decision. The applicant stabbed a female cyclist in the back in a life-threatening manner for sexual gratification. He then broke into a house, strangulated a four-year-old girl and injured her with a knife below the waist. He was diagnosed with sexual deviance and psycho-organic syndrome. The court endorsed the experts’ finding that the applicant’s personality disorder could no longer be treated because his sexually deviant aggressive behaviour had lasted for decades and because he would be unable to pursue psychotherapy. Public security could therefore be better safeguarded by placing the applicant in preventive detention. The applicant served his full term of imprisonment, and on 12 June 2001 he was placed for the first time in preventive Detention. The courts responsible for the execution of sentences ordered the continuation of the applicant’s preventive detention at regular intervals. By 11 June 2011 he had served ten years in preventive detention. The Lüneburg Regional Court further ordered the Rosdorf Prison authorities to offer the applicant, within three months of the date on which its decision became final, a specific anti-hormonal therapy with medication aimed at reducing his sadistic fantasies and his libido. The court had consulted the Celle Prison authorities and the prosecution and had heard the applicant in person as well as his counsel, who represented him throughout the proceedings before the domestic courts. The Regional Court found that, as required by section 316f(2), second sentence, of the Introductory Act to the Criminal Code, there was still a very high risk that, owing to specific circumstances relating to his personality and his conduct, the applicant would if released commit the most serious sexually motivated violent offences. Expert W. had confirmed that the applicant suffered from sexual sadism, a sexual deviance, and was addicted to alcohol, even though he had not drunk since being detained. The Regional Court considered that the prolongation of the preventive detention of the applicant, who had been detained for almost thirty years, was still proportionate in view of the considerable threat he posed. On 2 September 2013 the Celle Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal. Endorsing the reasons given by the Regional Court, it confirmed that the requirements laid down in section 316f(2), second sentence, of the Introductory Act to the Criminal Code for ordering the continuation of the applicant's preventive detention had been met. The court found that a mental disorder under that Act did not require that the disorder was such as to diminish or exclude the criminal responsibility of the person concerned for the purposes of Articles 20 and 21 of the criminal Code (see paragraphs 61-62 below). Specific disorders affecting a person's personality, conduct, sexual preference and control of impulses were covered by the notion of “mental disorder” in section 1(1) of the Therapy Detention Act. On 5 December 2011 the Lüneburg Regional Court, civil section, ordered the applicant’s placement in Moringen Psychiatric Hospital. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint without giving reasons (file no. 2 BvR 2182/13) The decision was served on the applicant ‘s counsel on 7 November 2013’. The decision of the Federal constitutional Court was published on 14 November 2013. It is based on a decision by the Court of Appeal in Celle, which upheld the Regional Court decision to place the applicant in a psychiatric hospital in December 2011. The Court of appeal found that the detention was still proportionate, despite the considerable overall length of his detention. Until 20 February 2012 the applicant had been held in preventive detention in a wing of Celle Prison. He had participated in therapy with a psychologist between 2005 and 2010, but had then stopped that therapy. He stopped attending a group for addicts and refused to take medication to reduce his libido for fear of side effects. The applicant has been detained in the new Rosdorf centre for prisoners since 2 June 2013. The conditions of the applicant’s preventive detention prior to the period of detention at issue are described below. The aim was to improve the available treatment options in the light of the duty to differentiate preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment. The conception of preventive detention in the centre was developed in order to comply with the constitutional requirement to differentiate between preventive detention and imprisonment. Detainees are placed in apartment units measuring some 23 square metres containing two furnished rooms and a bathroom. The rooms are equipped with a controlled access to the internet including e-mail, telephone, television, CD and DVD player and radio. There are common rooms for residential groups consisting of some seven detainees, which include a kitchen, a dining room, a television room and rooms for games, handicraft work and exercise. The outdoor premises, measuring some 1,600 square metres, can be used for sports, recreation or gardening. Persons in preventive detention may work, but are not obliged to do so. The applicant stopped participating in group sessions aimed at preventing relapsing into excessive alcohol consumption in August 2014. The applicant was accused of causing Yugoslavia’s welfare institutions to sustain substantial losses with the complicity of an official at the consulate of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Geneva. On 27 October 1982 he was arrested and charged with fraud, intimidation and forging documents. On 1 February 1984 the applicant paid the stipulated sum and was released. He then travelled to the United States of America, where he acquired American nationality and practised as a doctor specialising in the treatment of certain serious forms of cancer. The applicant was sentenced to life in prison in April 1989. The trial of the applicant was to begin on 17 April 1989 at the Canton of Geneva Assize Court. A Swiss doctor sought to stop treating an American patient. The American court issued a restraining order prohibiting the applicant from leaving the territory of the United States. The Swiss authorities were given sixty days to respond to the American court’s order. The applicant's lawyers made several applications for an adjournment of the trial, on 30 March and 4 April 1989. On 19 April 1989 the President of the Assize Court declined to adjourn the trial. He found that it had not been proved that the accused had been unable to attend the trial for a reason beyond beyond good cause. The trial began on 17 April 1989 at the Canton of Geneva Assize court. In a judgment of 26 May 1989 the Canton of Geneva Assize Court convicted the applicant in absentia and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment. The applicant was also found guilty of forgery of documents for procuring the signing by his secretary of seventeen false receipts for expenses in a name she no longer used. The jury assessed the amount of alleged damage at approximately 1,000,000 Swiss francs. On the other hand, the applicant was acquitted by the jury on 672 counts of fraud. On 26 April 1989 the applicant lodged an application with the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina to have the restraining order of 28 March 1989 set aside. In reply to a request by the applicant for a hearing date, the District Court informed him that it would not be able to examine the merits of the application for another thirty to sixty days. An application for the applicant’s immediate arrest made by the Principal Public Prosecutor after the delivery of the verdict was dismissed by the Assize Court. The offences to which the convictions related had been committed between 1973 and 1981. The applicant lodged an application with the Court of Justice of the Canton of Geneva for the conviction in absentia to be set aside, under Article 331 of the Geneva Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 42 below) He maintained that good cause had been shown for his absence at the hearing on 17 April 1989, as he had been compelled to comply with the enforceable decision of the American court – which clearly constituted a reason beyond his control. The applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation against the judgment of the. Court of Justice of 20 November 1989 dismissing his application for relief. The appeal had been lodged on 26 April 1989, that is to say a week after his trial had actually begun, and his. application for an adjournment had been dismissed. By that juncture, for reasons of time, he could no longer reverse the course of events he had helped set in motion. It held that the applicant’s inability to appear before the Assize Court was his own fault in that he had made a decisive contribution to that outcome. Further evidence of his bad faith was provided by the fact that he misled the American court about the procedure that would be followed in the criminal proceedings. The applicant lodged a public-law appeal with the Federal Court. He alleged, inter alia, a violation of his right to be heard and to attend his trial. The Federal Court dismissed his appeal. It held that Article 6 § 1 of the Convention did not preclude a trial being held in the defendant’s absence if the defendant refused to attend or was unable to attend through his or her own fault. It considered that the applicant had misled the American court by making inaccurate statements, notably regarding Swiss procedure, in order to secure a judgment making it impossible for him to attend. The Court of Cassation rejected the applicant's argument concerning the legal definition of the offences of fraud and forging documents. The applicant was arrested at Munich Airport (Germany) on his way to a conference in July 1995. He was extradited to Switzerland and transferred to Champ-Dollon Prison. An application he made for a pardon was refused in February 1996. He served the remainder of his sentence, spending part of it in a secure wing of Geneva Cantonal Hospital. On 20 December 1996 he returned to the United States. The Federal Court's opinion was that it was the applicant’s own fault that he had been unable to attend his trial. He had not given the American court accurate information about the procedure that would be followed or the sentence the applicant would face.

The court will consider the application's merits and whether or not it should be allowed to proceed with the application.

A single woman in Turkey sought to adopt a child, E., born on 5 November 2003. The registrar refused to indicate the applicant’s forename under the heading ‘mother’, where the name “S.” was retained. She argued that in relation to single-parent adoptions there was a lacuna in the Civil Code which required the court to make provision for such a situation of its own motion. The court dismissed her request on the ground that it had no legal basis. On 14 April 2008 the applicant appealed on points of law. In a decision of 22 May 2007, the applicant, who was then single, was authorised to adopt a child, E., born on 5 November 2003 to Ms S.Ö. The registrar refused to indicate the applicant’s forename under the heading ‘mother’, where the name “S.” was retained, this being the forename of the child's biological mother. In her view, the fact that her forename had not been given as that of the mother of her adopted son was both discriminatory and unconstitutional, likely to undermine their personal, family and social development, and thus constituting a violation of Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention.

A single mother wanted to adopt her son. The registrar refused to give her the forename of the boy's mother. The applicant appealed the decision. The court found that the Civil Code intended to treat the legal relationship between the adoptive parents and the adopted child as ‘a biological relationship’. A new regulation entered into force on 15 March 2009, enabling a single adoptive mother to adopt the child. The case was settled in the Turkish Supreme Court of Justice (TSK) in February 2009. The decision was delivered by the presiding judge, who was also the judge in the case of the adoption of a child by a single mother in 2003.

The new law allows a child to have his or her forename registered in the place of that of the biological parent. The application was made on 9 November 2010. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. The judge ruled that the application was not valid because of the new law, and that the applicant was not entitled to use her name for the purposes of the law. The decision was upheld on appeal on 5 November 2009, and the applicant appealed again on 14 December 2009. The appeal was dismissed on 2 January 2010.

The application was rejected by the Court of Cassation on 5 November 2009 in a judgment which made no mention of the legislative reform. The applicant was notified of that judgment on 14 December 2009. The child's name was then registered in the place of that of his or her biological parent. Landlord initiated proceedings before the Rent Review Board (hyresnämnden) in Stockholm against the applicants and some other tenants who had installed satellite dishes in the same house. Landlord sought execution of the notice of termination, claiming that the applicants' satellite installation violated the express ban in Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. In its place they installed a new device by placing on the kitchen floor an iron stand from which an arm, on which the satellite dish was mounted, extended through a small open window. The installation could be pulled back into the kitchen when not being used. At the request of the Tenants' Association, an engineer, Mr S. Tornefelt, examined the installation on 26 August 2004 and found that it was very stable. The Rent Review Board gave a decision on 21 October 2004 finding in their favour. The landlord appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt) The court held an oral hearing at which, inter alia, Mr Tornefelt gave evidence. It also made an inspection of the applicants' satellite installation. By a final decision of 20 December 2005, the court found that the applicants had disregarded their obligations as tenants, under the tenancy agreement and Chapter 12, section 25 of the Land Code, to such a degree that the agreement should not be extended. The applicants' interest in being able to watch television programmes not accessible by other available means weighed more heavily. The court found that the applicants' dish was virtually always positioned outside the kitchen window and thus constituted a permanent installation. The court considered that the landlord was entitled to make general risk assessments and should not have to determine whether an individual installation was unsafe or inconvenient. Although their satellite installation did not pose any real safety threat, their interests could not be allowed to override the weighty and reasonable interest of the landlord that order and good custom be upheld. eval_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two British nationals, Mark William Grayson and John Barnham. Each applicant alleged that, in confiscation proceedings following his conviction for drugs offences, the fact that the legal burden of proof was on him to show that he did not have realisable assets equivalent to the benefit figure offended the basic principles of a fair procedure. The Court decided to examine the merits of each application at the same time as its admissibility. It also decided to join the applications (Rule 42 § 1). Judge: 'I was satisfied that the applicant had been the principal participant in the offence and must have contributed to a large extent to the purchase of the drugs' 'The judge was further satisfied that so large a consignment would not have represented the applicant’s first venture into drug trafficking and that he had financed the purchase with the proceeds of previous drug dealing' He concluded that the. applicant had benefited to the amount of GBP 1,230,748.69 from the sale of drugs. The judge found that it was the applicant's money and that it showed he had money elsewhere he was not prepared to reveal. The police had found realisable assets of GBP 236,000, including the cash found on the applicant at the time of his arrest, a car and some business stock. The judge observed: “The fact that the police have traced a certain amount of property is not of itself a reason to find it is the only property available to the [applicant]. Also credibility is a real issue. This Defendant is cunning, devious and intelligent. Giving evidence he sought to mislead at every turn, wary that the truth would reveal assets he didn’t want to and that he had hidden assets prior to conviction. He has lied persistently and blatantly and his credibility is nil’ Court of Appeal referred to Phillips v. the United Kingdom, no. 41087/98, ECHR 2001-VII. Court added that the accountancy report. which the applicant sought to have admitted did not rebut the prosecution case but in. fact, to a large extent, supported it. “In that case the court held that the reverse onus of proof in relation to the statutory assumption at the calculation of the benefit stage is fully Convention compliant.” The second applicant (Mr Barnham) was convicted of two conspiracy charges involving plans to import large consignments of cannabis into the UK in 2001. The judge followed the scheme of the Act in arriving at his conclusions, and in the context of a man caught when engaged in importing heroin. The applicant was sentenced to eleven years’ imprisonment, the judge describing him as the lead organiser in a sophisticated, established and internationally based drug trafficking business. He did not give evidence but conceded through his counsel that he had benefited from drug trafficking within the meaning of the 1994 Act. The judge ruled that the total benefit to the applicant was GBP 1,525,615. This sum included GBP 27,000 that the applicant had given to Murray to establish his trust; various amounts totalling GBP 59,000 which he had mentioned to Murray during their conversations; a car worth GBP 11,615; and GBP 65,000 spent on renovating his house. The defence submitted that there was no evidence capable of supporting a finding of assumed ‘hidden’ assets. The judge found that the applicant and his wife had lied about their activities and their sources of income. The judge made a confiscation order equal to the amount which he had assessed as the benefit, namely GBP 1,525,615, with five years, three months’ imprisonment if the applicant had not paid within 18 months. The applicant appealed against the judge’s ruling regarding his realisable assets, asserting that Article 6 of the 1994 Act had been breached. The Court upheld the appeal and found the applicant to be guilty of conspiracy to import cannabis from Morocco to the UK. He was sentenced to five years and three months in prison. Court of Appeal found that the judge had made an error of calculation and reduced the order to GBP 1,460,615. Court of Appeal rejected this argument, holding as follows: ‘In our judgment the correct approach for the court to take when dealing with confiscation proceedings at the second stage is the same whether the benefit has been proved by evidence in addition to the statutory assumptions’ The expression ‘hidden assets’ is indicative of the fact that the prosecution can have no means of knowing how and where a defendant may have dealt with or disposed of the proceeds of his criminal activities. If he proves that he has no, or appreciably less, realisable assets than the amount of the benefit determined by the court the order will be made in a lesser sum. Court of Appeal refused to certify a point of law of general public importance for appeal to the House of Lords concerning Article 6 of the Convention. The Court of Appeal ruled that Article 6 was of 'general public importance' but not of 'public interest' The case was heard in front of the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled that the Convention should be extended to include Article 6. The appeal was thrown out by the European court of human rights, but the case was re-heard by the High Court of Justice. The court ruled in favor of Article 6, and the appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court of England and Wales, who ruled that it was of public interest.

The trial subsequently commenced in the Crown Court in June 2000. After the jury had already retired to consider their verdict a prejudicial document was discovered within the jury bundle. The fault for this lay with the prosecution, a matter admitted at the time. Consequently, on 31 August 2000 the jury were discharged. The 1994 Act provides for the making of a confiscation order in the event of a conviction for drug trafficking offences. On 6 June 2001 he was sentenced to fourteen years’ imprisonment. He lodged an appeal against sentence, which was unsuccessful. In 2004 he lodged an out-of-time appeal against conviction. He was released from prison in February 2006 and, on 17 November 2006, he abandoned his appeal (see further paragraph 29 below) The confiscation proceedings against the applicant were adjourned until the end of the year. eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the public prosecution office had collected and stored information about his professional bank account in a manner which was disproportionate. The German Federal Bar Association (Bundesrechtsanwaltskammer) was granted leave by the Vice‑President to intervene as third party. The application was communicated to the Government on 3 February 2016. The case was heard on 25 November 2013, and the jury found in favour of the applicant on 5 December 2013. The verdict was delivered on 9 February 2014, with the jury's decision to uphold the applicant’s right to appeal. The public prosecutor asked for a list of all transactions concerning the applicant’s bank account from 1 January 2009 until that day. He based his request for information on Articles 161a, 51 and 70 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (hereinafter ‘the CCP’) The public prosecutor did not order the bank to submit the information, but pointed to the obligations of witnesses set out in the CCP and the possible consequences of non‑compliance. A list of fifty-three transactions deemed to be relevant was included in the investigation file as evidence. The bank complied with both requests for information and submitted the information to the public prosecution office. The applicant, as the lawyer of the accused, was granted access to the investigation file. From the case file he learned, for the first time, of the investigative measures concerning his own bank account. He asked the Chief Public Prosecutor to hand over to him all data received from the bank and destroy all related data at the public prosecution office. In his request the applicant emphasised his role as a criminal defence lawyer, which was known to the acting public prosecutor, and the consequences for his clients, whose names were accessible through the banking information. The applicant appealed against the decision. The court found that the investigation was lawful, that the bank had provided the information voluntarily and that the documents could therefore only be returned to the bank. The Hamm Court of Appeal confirmed the decision of the Regional Court on 13 September 2012. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant’s constitutional complaint, without providing reasons (case no. 2 BvR 2268/12) The judge said that the bank could not be considered a person assisting the applicant or a person involved in the professional activities of the applicant under Article 53a of the CCP (see paragraph 27 below). The judge added that there were several safeguards in place concerning the seizure of documents (see paragraphs 26-29 below), and these should not have been circumvented because his and his clients' personal information was stored at and by the bank, and not at his office.

On 6 December 1991 Ms Halford applied to the Interception of Communications Tribunal (‘the Tribunal’) for an investigation under section 7 of the 1985 Act. In a letter dated 21 February 1992, the Tribunal informed her that its investigation had satisfied it that there had been no contravention of sections 2 to 5 of the Act in her case. The Tribunal confirmed that it could not specify whether any interception had in fact taken place (see paragraph 32 below). In August 1992, Home Secretary David Alton MP explained that the Home Secretary’s complaint regarding the interception of calls made from her office telephones “[did] not fall within [his] responsibilities as Home Secretary nor within the terms of the [1985] Act“

Mr Dominique Veuillet: 'We knew that Mr Ankerl was in de facto occupation of the premises' 'We had informed him about the proposed works in the building' 'He told me that he did not wish to proceed in the matter' 'I sent the file to our lawyer, who must have informed him of the shareholder’s position' 'My office staff must, it would seem, have communicated our account number to Mr Ankersl' 'At that time, as far as we were concerned, his position remained as we had described in our letter of 14 July 1987' 'There was no evidence of a breach of any law or contract of any kind' Mr Ruffieux: Mr Linder never asked us to look for a flat elsewhere. He did not indicate that we had to leave within a given time. I myself had the impression that he had some freedom of action. Mr Ankerl: When I concluded the lease with Régie Immobilière, I did not realise that it was a subtenancy. He is up to date with the rent. I would not have been opposed to a settlement at the outset but relations with Mr An Kearl have become difficult.“On 12 October 1989 the court held that there was no lease agreement between the parties and ordered Mr Ankersl to move all property and persons from the flat. Mr Linder, an employee of the new management, told the Court that he had had an interview with Mr Ankerl and had made it clear to him that in his view he did not have a lease. Mr Ruffieux, the director and shareholder of the plaintiffs, said he had never agreed, and did not wish to agree, to enter into a lease with the defendant. In the instant case no lease has been signed since the termination of the sublease. The Court reaches the conclusion that no lease was entered into orally (the existence of an oral agreement has not been proved) or even implied by the clear conduct of the parties. Guy Ankerl was denied a lease by Chrysanthemum SA. He appealed to the Canton of Geneva Court of Justice. The appeal was dismissed. The applicant lodged a public-law appeal in the Federal Court of France. The case was heard in the Court of First Instance and the appeal was rejected. The defendant is on the premises unlawfully. Article 641 para. 2 [of the Civil Code] applies in this case ...“. The sublease is a lease between the tenant and the subtenant. ... Having been given notice for 28 February 1988, Guy AnkerL, from that date, no longer has any right to remain on the. premises. ... “The equality of arms guaranteed both in the Federal Constitution and in the European Convention on Human Rights was not ensured.’ The First Civil Division of the Federal Court delivered its judgment on 3 October 1990. It declared inadmissible - in particular - the complaint based on a violation of Articles 6 and 14 of the Convention (art. 6, art. 14) of which the appellant makes a bald assertion without providing any explanation.“If the appellant’s argument, which is not very clear, has been understood correctly, the cantonal appellate court inadmissibly took into account the interview that Mr Linder had with the appellant in April 1988 in the presence of the appellant's wife, in that it completely ignored her statements.” The appellant’s wife was heard only for information purposes and without taking the oath. The court below did not infer from those statements that the witness had indicated to the appellant that he would have to leave the flat. ... The present appeal is manifestly ill-founded, and it must accordingly be dismissed in so far as it is admissible.“Mr and Mrs Ankerl left the flat in issue on 16 October 1991. The applicant’'s departure from the flat was at the end of October 1991 ... The appellant did not attack that finding. It merely found that Mr Linder `confirmed that he. would pass on to the landlord Guy Ankerls’ wish to enter into a new lease’.

The applicant was taken into police custody by the Anti-Terror branch of the Istanbul Security Directorate on suspicion of being a member of the PKK. He claims that during his interrogation, he was blindfolded and stripped naked. He was strung up by his arms in the form of torture known as “Palestinian hanging” His head was hit against the wall and he was held parallel to the ground on his hands and feet. The Government submit that the applicant was questioned by the police on 15 July 1994. According to the medical report prepared by Dr Apaydın, the applicant showed no signs of ill-treatment. eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that there had been a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Court declared the application admissible in November 2003. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine), the parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The Secretary of State for Trade and Industry applied for an extension of time for the serving of evidence (see below) The applicant and three other defendants in the Blackspur proceedings had been brought against them on 1 July 1992. The Secretary of State’s evidence was completed and served on the applicant on 14 December 1992. On 13 May 1993 the applicant applied to strike out the proceedings. At the conclusion of the criminal trial, the applicant and one other defendant were acquitted, and two defendants were convicted. On appeal, the two convictions were quashed in February 1995. In November 1995 Mr Davies was granted leave to appeal out of time to the Court of Appeal, and his substantive appeal was dismissed by that court on 24 May 1996. The appeal to the High Court brought by the first defendant to the disqualification proceeding was dismissed on 2 May 1995. The defendants were ordered to serve their evidence by 17 January 1997. They failed to comply and the case was adjourned until 9 February 1998. On 17 February 1998 the defendants told the Secretary of State that they were willing to settle the case. They did so on 18 November 1997. The case was then reopened and the defendants were allowed to give their evidence. The defendants were found not guilty of any charges. They were then allowed to continue the case until the end of March 1998. The hearing was called to determine whether the case should be referred to the High Court. The High Court ruled that it was not in the public interest for the case to continue. The applicant tried to negotiate a ‘Carecraft’ settlement with the Secretary of State. The Secretary of state agreed to a five-year period of disqualification. On 23 March 1998 the time-limit for the applicant’s further evidence was extended indefinitely. The applicant applied for judicial review of the legality of the decision of 30 June 1999, not to discontinue the proceedings on grounds of delay. The matter was set down for trial on 4 October 1999. On 2 February 2000, the applicant renewed his judicial review application before the Court of Appeal. It was refused by the Court. of Appeal on 15 March 2000, following an oral hearing. Lord Justice Buxton described the application as ‘misconceived’. The applicant appealed to the House of Lords, which granted leave on 11 July 2000. The House heard the applicant’s appeal on 18 October 2000, and on 2 November 2000 delivered judgment dismissing it. The application was heard by the Vice-Chancellor on 7 February 2001, and judgment was delivered dismissing it on 15 February 2001. In the judgments of the Court of Appeal given in November 1997, Mr Eastaway was denied leave to apply for judicial review. Those actions were taken not to obtain but to avoid a fair and public hearing by an independent or impartial tribunal either within a reasonable time or at all. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43626/98) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained that he had been held in detention arbitrarily. He had been kept in custody even though the order extending his detention had expired. By a decision of 31 August 2000 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Court’s decision is obtainable from the Registry. The Government, but not the applicant, filed further written observations on the merits of the case (Rule 59 § 1) in October 2000. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal in Paris in October 2001. The applicant was charged with armed robbery, false imprisonment, and wounding with intent and wilful violence. A forged identity card bearing the applicant’s photo was discovered, together with a sawn-off shotgun. An employee admitted that he had provided the applicant with information to help him commit the armed robbery in return for the sum of FRF 10,000. He also stated that he recognised the applicant while the offence was being committed despite the mask he had been wearing and that the applicant was the robber who had been carrying the sawnoffs. The judge substituted for the charge of false imprisonment with voluntary release (an intermediate offence (délit) and made a partial discharge order. The applicant claimed he had lodged a complaint with the Créteil public prosecutor alleging arbitrary detention but had received no reply. On 9 April 1997 the applicant made an application to the Indictment Division for his immediate release on the ground that he was being detained arbitrarily. In a judgment of 19 August 1997 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on the following grounds: “It appears from the impugned judgment and the documents on the file that on 19 January 1995 a warrant of commitment was issued in respect of [the applicant], who was under investigation for offences including armed robbery’” The application was refused in the judgment now appealed against on the grounds that the investigating court did not lay itself open to the objections raised. The initial warrant of commitment remained effective, in accordance with Article 181, second paragraph, of the Code, after the transfer order was issued. An appeal on points of law by the applicant against that judgment was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 18 December 1997. On 9 and 10 June 1998 the applicant was tried at the Versailles Assize Court, which sentenced him to ten years’ imprisonment. The applicant was ordered to pay the civil party FRF 50,000 in damages in a judgment delivered on the same day on the civil claims. In a. judgment of 3 March 1999 the Court of Cassation dismissed appeals on points of law by the applicant against the Assize Court’s judgments.

The second applicant already had three children from other relationships. In October 2001 the first applicant applied for facilities for artificial insemination. In December 2002 the secondApplicant joined this application. Their solicitors made representations to the Secretary of State, relying on the length of the relationship and the fact that it was unlikely that the applicants would be able to have a child together. In a letter dated 28 May 2003 the secretary of state refused their application.

The applicants were born in 1972 and 1958. The first applicant is in prison (Dovergate Prison, Uttoxeter) and the second applicant lives in Hull. In October 2001 the first applicant applied for facilities for artificial insemination. The second applicant joined this application in December 2002. Their solicitors made representations to the Secretary of State, relying on the length of the relationship and the fact that it was unlikely that the applicants would be able to have a child together. In a letter dated 28 May 2003 the secretary of state refused their application. He first set out his general policy (‘the policy’): ‘Requests for artificial Insemination by prisoners are carefully considered on individual merit and will only be granted in exceptional circumstances’

Both applicants were in full agreement about their wish to conceive artificially. The relationship was established while they were in prison and had not been tested in the normal environment of daily life. There was insufficient provision in place to provide independently for the material welfare of any child which might be conceived. Fifthly, in light of the violence of the first applicant’s crime, there would be legitimate public concern that the punitive and deterrent elements of his sentence of imprisonment were being circumvented if he were allowed to father a child by artificial insemination. The applicants then applied to the Court of Appeal for leave to appeal. On 30 September 2004 their application was unanimously rejected.

Auld LJ noted that on occasions the Secretary of State had “dis-applied the policy’ when the circumstances had merited it. The starting point of the policy is that deprivation of facilities for artificial insemination may prevent conception altogether. The finishing point is whether there are exceptional circumstances for not applying the policy. It is not open to [the applicants] to seek to re-open the validity of the Secretary. of State’s policy which this court has held in Mellor is rational and otherwise lawful. The Supreme Court said the public interest was at stake in the case. The applicants, who were granted legal aid, were represented by Mr E. Abrahamson, a lawyer practising in Liverpool. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government’s” Agent) was represented by their Agent, Mr J. Grainger, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The first applicant was convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment with a tariff of 15 years. He is imprisoned in a private prison and his earliest expected release date is 2009. The second applicant already had three children from other relationships. The judge gives his reasons for refusal in the present case. ‘On the one hand, the second applicant would be 51 years old at the earliest possible date of release of the first applicant so that the likelihood of her being able to conceive naturally was small. Both applicants were also in full agreement about their wish to conceive artificially. However, on the other hand, and in the first place, the relationship was established while they were in prison and had not been tested in the normal environment of daily life’ ‘There was insufficient provision in place to provide independently for the material welfare of any child which might be conceived. Fourthly, any child would be without a father for an important part of its childhood years’ Auld LJ relied in principle on the judgment of the Court of Appeal in R (Mellor) v Secretary of State for the Home Department ([2001] 3 WLR 533). train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 15737/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the applicant’s right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The Court ruled in favour of the applicant and the application was dismissed. The 2004 Act on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time (Ustawa o skardze na naruszenie prawa strony do rozpoznania sprawy w postępowaniu sądowym) entered into force on 17 September 2004. It lays down various legal means designed to counteract and/or redress the undue length of judicial proceedings. A party to pending proceedings may ask for the acceleration of those proceedings under section 2 read in conjunction with section 5(1) of the 2004 Act. The Supreme Court ruled that while the 2004 Law produced legal effects as from the date of its date of entry into force (17 September 2004), its provisions applied retroactively to all proceedings in which delays had occurred before that date.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30054/96) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants were next-of-kin of nine men killed during a security force operation at Loughgall on 8 May 1987. They alleged that their relatives had been kill unjustifiably, without any attempt being made to bring them before a court. They invoked Articles 2, 6, 14 and 13 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The case was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). The Human Rights Commission was given leave by the President to intervene in the written procedure. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building on 4 April 2000. The applicants accepted that the summaries below are an accurate reflection of the written statements made by the official personnel involved, without making any admission as to the credibility, consistency and veracity of these statements. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court heard addresses by Mr Weatherup and Mr Korff. The Chamber declared the application admissible. The application was made on behalf of a group of soldiers who had been involved in a raid on Loughgall station in the early hours of 8 May 1987. Two hooded men hijacked a blue Toyota Hiace van from a Mr Corr. He was warned not to report the incident to the police for four hours. Three armed men who said they were from the IRA entered the house of the Mackle family in Aghinlig Upper, Dungannon. The men said they wanted to borrow the digger and one of the sons was brought outside to fill it with diesel. At about 6.30 p.m., a vehicle pulled up outside and a fourth man arrived. It appears that a bomb containing 300 to 400 pounds of explosives was prepared in the yard of the house. The incident at Loughgall took place between 7.15 and 7.30 p.m. The soldiers reported a number of sightings of the blue Hiace van passing in front of the RUC station in both directions. Reports that the van had been hijacked, and that a digger was acting suspiciously in the area, were also received. Given this information and the knowledge that diggers had been used in previous terrorist attacks, the soldiers were on full alert when the incident occurred. The digger stopped and shortly afterwards there was an explosion which caused masonry and dust to fly everywhere. Soldiers A to F and Constable A were unhurt by the blast which damaged a large part of the station. Soldiers A, B, D and E moved towards the front of the RUC station and continued to fire at the men near the van. Soldier F also left the station by the rear and did not take any part in the shooting. Constables B and C were led outside by Constable A and Soldier C, who administered first aid to them. Shortly after the bomb exploded, Soldiers K and R observed what they thought was a gunman lying in the grass behind the police station. He failed to stand up when challenged to do so, and both soldiers fired several rounds at what turned out to be a large lump of wood. Soldier V fired at a man in a blue boiler suit crossing the road in a crouched manner. The man moved away quickly, then turned fully towards Soldier V who saw something in his hand which he regarded as an immediate threat. When the soldiers and members of the RUC. were airlifted back to their barracks. The first body (Patrick Kelly) was found lying on his back still moving. The driver of the car was dead at the wheel of the vehicle. Other vehicles near the scene of the attack included a red Sierra 15 metres from position 6, occupied by a woman and her daughter. A blue Escort about 70 metres from the scene which was empty and a white Sierra, with three female occupants. These cars, or their occupants, were directed to positions of safety by soldiers as soon as the opportunity arose. There were two significantly bullet damaged vehicles, a blue Toyota Hiace van with approximately 125 bullet holes in the bodywork. In the vicinity of the junction of Clovenden Road/Ballygasey Road there were bullet damaged Vauxhall Cavalier and Ford estate cars. Debris on the rifle suggests that this person was lying on the ground before the explosion. There were four loaded rifles and one shotgun found in the van. The sixth body had massive head damage and multiple injuries elsewhere. The seventh body was not wearing a boiler suit and there was a cigarette lighter close to the right hand. The eighth body (Gerald O’Callaghan) was. lying on its right side on the pavement at the Loughgall side of the lane-way. Twelve wounds were noted by the pathologist. The post mortem examination revealed at least a dozen wounds to the torso and head. The ninth body (Antony Hughes) was seated with the seat belt on in the driver’s seat of the white Citroen car. The body was not wearing a boiler suit. The post mortem examination showed twenty-nine wounds (bullet and shrapnel) Spent cartridge cases were recovered from all over the crime scene which stretched from the junction of Cloveneden Road/Ballygasey Road to the Church/Church Hall in the vicinity of the start of Main Street, Loughgall. The inquest was adjourned on 6 September 1990, pending the determination of the Devine case, before the Court of Appeal (and subsequently the House of Lords), which concerned the powers of Coroners. Inquest into the deaths of the four men was held in May 1995. The families of the victims asked for the statements of prospective witnesses to be made available at the start of the hearing. The request was refused and the families withdrew from the hearing on 31 May. The inquest was eventually adjourned for two months. The bodies of the men were never recovered. The trial was adjourned until the 21st of November 2013. The case was referred to the High Court by the families as the ‘Case of the Death of the Four Men’. eval_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 52562/99 and 52620/99) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Rasmussen, Advisers. The Court heard addresses by Mr Lego Andersen and Mr TaksÃ¼e Jensen. The applicant became aware that he was paying a subscription to SID, although he had not applied for membership. Denmark's Free Trade Union (Danmarks Frie Fagforening) represented the applicant in the High Court of Western Denmark (Vestre Landsret) The High Court found for FDB, stating as follows: “The High Court finds it established that the applicant was aware that membership of SID was a condition for his employment in the company. Thus, since the applicant did not comply with this requirement the conditions for dismissing him are fulfilled in accordance with section 2, subsection (2), in conjunction with subsection (1), of the Protection against Dismissal due to Association Membership Act.” The question is whether the Act is at variance with Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, in the light of the interpretation this Article has been given by the European Court of Human Rights. Danish Supreme Court upheld the High Court's judgment on 8 June 1999. Case-law should disregard section 2(2) of the Protection against Dismissal due to Association Membership Act, the starting-point must be taken from the Act of 1992 incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant served his prison term until 24 May 2002. He did not benefit from early release. The application was dismissed by both the Administrative Court and the Constitutional Court. The Vienna Federal Police Authority ordered the applicant’s detention with a view to his expulsion in 2003 and he was deported to Bulgaria in 2004. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Austria, which ruled that the residence prohibition was justified under Article 8.

Most recently, in October 1996 he was sentenced to a one-year term of imprisonment for a serious forgery offence. The applicant requested the court, pursuant to the provisions of chapter 22 of the Code of Judicial Procedure (Rättegångsbalken: see paragraph 20 below), to order L. to pay him 169,350 Swedish kronor (SEK) in compensation. The applicant applied for compensation to the Criminal Damage Compensation Board (Brottsskadenämnden - hereinafter “the Board’) on 15 April 1993. In his application he stated that he had sought compensation for personal injury in the amount of SEK 160,000 in the proceedings against L. The Stockholm District Court convicted L., sentenced him to six years’ imprisonment and ordered him to pay SEK 144,350 in damages to the applicant. The Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt) reversed the District Court’s decision on the ground that the charges against L had not been proven, acquitted L and rejected the applicant's claim for compensation. The Board rejected the applicant’s compensation claim on 26 August 1993. The applicant requested the Board to reconsider its decision. He argued that it was clear from the judgments of the District Court and the Court of Appeal that he had been the victim of a crime. He had identified two of the three persons who were allegedly involved in the offences; the fact that the only one to be charged, L., was guilty was not a reason to doubt that he was a victim of crime. The Board decided that it could not find it established that [the applicant] has suffered damage as a result of crime, and that compensation for damage caused by crime cannot be awarded. Inspector S. had been the principal investigator into the economic offences of which the applicant had previously been convicted. He had interrogated both the applicant and L. on a number of occasions. In May 1992 the applicant mentioned the kidnappings when he was being interrogated as a suspect in another case. He stated that [they had been carried out] by two black men and a third one, whom he did not wish to name. In the autumn [of 1991] he named one of the assistants [during the kidnapping], [P.] ... [The applicant’s description of the environment and premises where he had been kept during the kidnapping] was very accurate as regards many details. On 1 June 1994 the Board rejected the applicant’s request, for the following reasons: “The submissions in this case in support of the request for reconsideration are not such as to be a reason for the Board to change its previous decision. Nor is there any other reason for changing the decision.” “He had more or less repeated the same evidence he gave to the District Court.“ “There was no reason to change the previous decision,” said the Board. “ nor was there any reason to make a new decision in relation to this case.’ “ ‘The applicant had provided no new evidence. He had provided the same. evidence as he had previously provided.

After the judge's decision, the mother was allowed to keep it on. The mother now wants to wear it again. The judge said she should not have been allowed to wear the scarf in the first place. The woman's application was denied, and the case was returned to the Court of Appeal. The appeal was heard on 11 March 2013. The decision was upheld. The applicant's parents lodged an appeal on points of law with the Conseil d'Etat, relying, inter alia, on their daughter's right to freedom of conscience and expression. On 31 July 2003 the Nantes Administrative Court of Appeal dismissed their appeal, on the same grounds as the lower court, finding that the applicant, by behaving as she had done, had overstepped the limits of the right to express and manifest her religious beliefs on the school premises. The applicant indicated that she subsequently took correspondence courses in order to continue her school studies. The application was filed on behalf of the applicant's minor daughter. The appeal was declared inadmissible by the Conseil d'Etat in December 2004. The appeal was brought by former French President Jacques Chirac. The case was later dismissed by the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg in March 2005. The Appeal was dismissed and the case was dismissed as "inadmissible" in April 2004. He and a co-accused (NB) were interviewed at length by police officers. Numerous questions were put to them concerning the events in Corke Abbey and the evidence gathered by the police. Neither answered any question. The trial court later noted that the two accused accepted that they had had full access to legal advice and found that each had availed himself of the opportunity to consult a solicitor before and during several police interviews. The SCC directed the Chief Superintendent to produce all relevant documentation which, he asserted, informed him that the accused were members of the IRA. The law says that a child is not entitled to an allowance unless he or she is under 16 years of age. The law was enacted after the death of a 16-year-old boy, who had been in the care of his mother. The child was born in April 1989. His mother, a mother-of-two, had to wait until he was 18 to claim an allowance. She could not do so until then, so the law was changed to allow for the mother to claim. The new law was approved by the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled in favor of the mother's right to a child's allowance. The mother, who was also a mother, was allowed to claim the money.

The law states that children under 12 are entitled to receive an allowance if they are not under the age of 14. The law was amended in the 1990s to make it clear that this does not apply to children under 16. The new law was brought in to make the provision for children born after January 1, 1990. It was the first time since 1970s that the law had been amended in this way. The decision was made on the basis that the change in the law did not affect the child’s right to be a child and it did not infringe on his or her right to an equal right to a fair trial.

The law was changed in April 1989. It said that only women can claim an allowance if they are pregnant or have a child. The law was later amended to allow fathers to claim the allowance if a child is born. However, the new law does not apply to fathers who are already fathers. The new law was brought in by the European Commission after the case was brought before the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg in 1989. The European Court ruled that the law is unconstitutional because it does not comply with the European Convention on Human Rights. The case was dismissed on the grounds that the legislation was not properly amended to make the change.

It originated in an application (no. 20458/92) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by an Austrian national, Mr Antun Petrovic, on 3 August 1992. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 14 taken together with Article 8 of the Convention. On 20 January 1997, in the presence of the Registrar, the President of the Court, Mr R. Ryssdal, drew by lot the names of the other seven members. Hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 October 1997. Court heard addresses by Mr Marxer, Mr Laimer and Mr Okresek. Commission produced various documents from the proceedings before it, as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions. The circumstances of the case were as follows: Mr Petrovic claimed a parental leave allowance (Karenzurlaubsgeld) His claim was turned down by the local employment office (Arbeitsamt) on the ground that section 26(1) of the Unemployment Benefit Act 1977 provided that only mothers could claim such an allowance when a child was born. On 12 December 1991, after considering the complaint in private, the Constitutional Court declined to accept it for adjudication on the ground that it did not have sufficient prospects of success. The Constitutional Court held that section 26(1) did not infringe the applicant’s constitutional rights and was not contrary to Article 8 or Article 12 of the Convention. It added that even if regard was had to recent statutory amendments (section 26 of the Unemployment Benefit Act had been amended by a federal law of 12 December 1989 – see paragraph 15 below), the applicant's complaint was unfounded, seeing that the legislature had a certain amount of time to adapt new rules to changes in society.

He had been reported to the police for embezzlement of the Democratic Alliance's funds. An audit had shown that he had transferred 1,340 Swedishkronor from the association's account to his own account.
